clinicalPearls: First described by Miyake, this dystrophy causes progressive bilateral central visual loss despite an essentially normal-looking fundus, hence occult
Frequently caused by RP1L1 mutations, most often autosomal dominant, though sporadic and recessive cases occur
The key diagnostic feature is a normal full-field electroretinogram with a selectively abnormal multifocal (or focal macular) electroretinogram, localising dysfunction to the central macula
Fluorescein angiography is typically normal, which historically made the condition difficult to diagnose before multifocal electroretinography and OCT
Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography reveals disruption or blurring of the ellipsoid zone and the interdigitation zone at the fovea, often the only structural clue
Colour vision and peripheral fields are usually preserved, and the diagnosis is easily missed as functional or non-organic visual loss
Management is supportive with low-vision aids and genetic counselling; there is no established treatment to reverse the macular dysfunction
reference.pathophysiology: Occult macular dystrophy is an inherited cone dysfunction confined to the central macula, commonly caused by mutations in RP1L1, a gene expressed in photoreceptors and important for outer-segment structure and function. The disorder selectively impairs the central cone photoreceptors while sparing the peripheral retina, so the standard full-field electroretinogram, which reflects the whole retina, remains normal, whereas the focal macular and multifocal electroretinogram are abnormal. Corresponding subtle disruption of the foveal ellipsoid and interdigitation zones on optical coherence tomography reflects the localised photoreceptor dysfunction, with a normal fundus and normal angiography throughout.
additionalDifferentials: Cone or cone-rod dystrophy (which show abnormal full-field electroretinography)
Stargardt disease and other maculopathies with visible changes
Central serous or other subtle maculopathies
additionalInvestigations: Multifocal and focal macular electroretinography demonstrating central dysfunction with a normal full-field electroretinogram
Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography for ellipsoid and interdigitation zone disruption at the fovea
Fundus autofluorescence, which may be near-normal, to help exclude other maculopathies
Fluorescein angiography, expected to be normal, to exclude vascular or inflammatory causes
Colour vision and visual field testing
Molecular genetic testing for RP1L1 and related genes
redFlags: Unexplained progressive central visual loss with a normal fundus that risks being dismissed as non-organic
Asymmetric or unilateral presentation prompting exclusion of an optic neuropathy
Rapid deterioration warranting prompt multifocal electroretinography and OCT
Affected relatives who may benefit from screening given frequent dominant inheritance
reference.prognosis: Central acuity declines slowly and progressively over years to a moderate low-vision level, while peripheral vision, colour vision and night vision are typically preserved.
pitfalls: Diagnosing non-organic or functional visual loss because the fundus, angiography and full-field electroretinogram are normal
Relying on full-field electroretinography alone and omitting multifocal or focal macular testing
Overlooking subtle foveal ellipsoid zone disruption on optical coherence tomography
Confusing it with an optic neuropathy in asymmetric cases
management: No disease-specific or curative treatment exists; management focuses on maximising and supporting residual central vision
Refractive correction and low-vision rehabilitation with magnifiers, high-contrast aids and optimised lighting
Serial monitoring with multifocal or focal macular electroretinography and spectral-domain optical coherence tomography to document slow progression
Referral to an inherited retinal disease service, with registration for emerging gene-directed therapy trials where relevant
Genetic counselling for the usually autosomal dominant RP1L1 disorder, with testing of at-risk relatives
Educational, occupational and psychological support, avoiding misdiagnosis as functional visual loss
